title: DfE Decoded 167 Your GLD Data Now Has Context
author: Paul Urry
summary: Paul Urry explains the new contextual Good Level of Development score now appearing alongside schools' Early Years data. Instead of comparing a school's GLD only with the national figure, the DfE uses a statistical model of a Reception cohort's characteristics to estimate the percentage expected to reach GLD, then compares that with actual results. The model draws on free school meals, SEN support, EHCPs, EAL, average age, IDACI deprivation, ethnicity, urban or rural home area, mobility and prior early education, plus whole-school SEN information. Urry stresses that the score is an estimate, not a target or minimum, and that the model explains only about half the variation between schools. He argues leaders should use it to start better questions about curriculum, provision and transition, whether results sit above or below the estimate, rather than to claim success or failure.
points: The contextual GLD score estimates the proportion of a Reception cohort expected to reach GLD, given its characteristics, and sets it beside the actual result.
The model accounts for a wide range of factors including cohort age, SEN support and EHCPs, mobility, EAL and neighbourhood deprivation rather than just free school meals.
The DfE states plainly that the score is not a target, minimum standard or precise prediction, and the model explains only about half of the variation between schools.
Results above the estimate should prompt leaders to ask what is working, and results below it should prompt the question of what needs to be understood better rather than why the school has failed.
The model leaves out factors such as attendance, funding, looked-after children and specialist SEN provision, so leaders still need to tell the fuller story.
quotes: It asks: “What might we reasonably expect the GLD outcome to look like for a cohort with characteristics like ours?” That is a very different question.
A September-born Reception child and an August-born Reception child may be almost twelve months apart developmentally. At four and five years old, that is enormous.
That does not mean lowering expectations for summer-born children. It means recognising that context exists.
A school cannot reasonably be expected to have had the same educational influence over a child who joined in April as one who has been there since September.
In fact, the final statistical model explains around half of the variation in GLD outcomes between schools.
Contextual data is better context. It is not complete context.
